Evaluation is restricted to six curated BMAD datasets, with segmentation assessed on only three. No independent multicenter, temporal, or prospective validation is reported, limiting evidence for broad clinical generalizability.

The leave-one-dataset-out protocol does not clarify whether RESC and OCT17 are withheld together. Since both contain retinal OCT images, retaining either during training would make evaluation on the other cross-dataset transfer rather than transfer to an unseen modality and anatomy.

The universal-model framing exceeds the demonstrated setting: leave-one-out runs and target-specific few-shot adaptation produce different fitted models, rather than establishing that one fixed model handles multiple previously unseen medical domains.

Zero-shot inference still requires supervised adaptation on medical source data, including pixel-level annotations where available. Few-shot image counts also understate dense-mask annotation effort, limiting practicality when labeled abnormalities or source masks are unavailable.

Patient-, volume-, and slide-level separation is not consistently documented, particularly for the labeled training pools. Slice and patch counts obscure the number of independent patients, leaving potential leakage and correlation effects insufficiently addressed.

No explicit unseen-pathology or leave-disease-out evaluation is provided, particularly after few-shot adaptation. Detecting benchmark-defined abnormalities does not establish reliable detection of genuinely novel disease types.

Random few-shot support-set selection is not accompanied by repeated-run statistics, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Sampling variance is therefore unknown, which is especially important for ensemble gains of only 0.13 classification and 0.05 segmentation AUC percentage points over the best individual level.

Evaluation relies exclusively on ROC-AUC, without Dice/IoU, PR-AUC, lesion-level sensitivity, false positives per scan, or performance at clinically relevant thresholds. High pixel-level AUC alone does not establish accurate lesion localization or useful clinical operating points.

Comparisons with full-normal-shot and few-normal-shot baselines change the supervision regime: MVFA receives labeled abnormalities and, where available, masks. These comparisons cannot isolate architectural gains from the benefit of abnormal supervision.

No equally parameterized image-only adapter baseline is trained with the same medical labels and multi-level losses. Consequently, the contribution of language alignment is not isolated from supervised visual adaptation and multi-level supervision.

Only CLIP ViT-L/14 is adapted. Medical-pretrained VLMs such as MedCLIP are not evaluated with matched MVFA adaptation, leaving portability across backbones and the advantage over equally adapted medical encoders untested.

The fixed 240-pixel input, coarse ViT patch grid, and bilinear map upsampling constrain spatial resolution. No lesion-size-stratified evaluation establishes whether small or subtle abnormalities survive resizing and coarse localization.

MRI and CT are evaluated as 2D slices, and histopathology as patches, without volumetric or whole-slide context or patient-level aggregation. Performance on complete clinical scans and slides remains unestablished.

The few-shot sampling protocol does not specify normal/abnormal balance or pathology coverage within each K-shot support set. This makes the amount of abnormal supervision and representativeness of the normal-feature memory bank difficult to assess.

The stated training objective requires pixel-level masks, but OCT17, ChestXray, and HIS provide only image labels. The paper does not explain how segmentation losses are handled for these datasets, leaving an important training-protocol ambiguity.

Few-shot fusion combines softmax scores with raw cosine distances using fixed 0.5 weights, without documented normalization or calibration. Their numerical scales need not match, and no fusion-weight sensitivity analysis establishes reliable transfer across domains.

Text prompts are manually engineered and incorporate target-organ names. Robustness to prompt wording, missing or incorrect organ metadata, and alternative clinically meaningful anomaly descriptions is not evaluated.

The lightweight claim lacks trainable-parameter counts, runtime, FLOPs, and memory comparisons. A large ViT-L/14 backbone and four-level nearest-neighbor searches remain at inference, so deployment efficiency and memory-bank scaling are unclear.

Benefits are not uniform: zero-shot BrainMRI segmentation trails April-GAN (90.27% versus 91.79% AUC), and two-shot LiverCT segmentation trails BGAD (96.57% versus 98.71%). Average gains and selected qualitative examples do not explain these failure modes.
